video_title: Why AI Can Write Code But Can’t Keep It Running (Yet)
gist: Greer CEO Jad and a16z's Martin Casado discuss how AI delivers 10-20x gains in production code but struggles with operations, where state spaces are vast, data is hidden, and they debate whether change-detection plus LLM reasoning can automate reliability.

insights.claim: A single senior engineer used Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to ship production data-lake auto-promotion (shredding log fields into columns) in about 10 days, work he says would have taken one person roughly 6 months.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Roughly 10-20x gains on complex production infrastructure code, not just demos.
insights.quote: Sort of like factor of 10, factor of 20 improvement.

insights.claim: Early AI coding was only autocomplete (Copilot, IntelliJ); it rapidly evolved to building complex software, breaking through expectations as models handled more system complexity.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Skeptic priors on AI capability have repeatedly been wrong in code, which should temper skepticism elsewhere.

insights.claim: AI amplifies engineering skill disparity: good engineers become far better while weaker engineers do not become good, because the gains depend on how much complexity one can hold in mind to decompose and assign tasks.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Talent spread widens; hiring bar and team structure should favor top engineers (observed on a small team doing distributed systems).
insights.quote: the more complexity that your brain can handle, the more you can break down the tasks and kind of assign them

insights.claim: Harness choice matters: different tools (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) manage context, sub-agents and prompts differently, and Claude Code will burn tokens spinning up many research agents unless told not to.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Harness-specific operating skill and token cost control are emerging engineering competencies.

insights.claim: Workflow trick: have Claude spin up command-line sub-agents rather than built-in sub-agents because they keep persistent sessions, saving context; a tech-lead reviewer agent reviews the implementer's PR doc and design doc before a human reviews them.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Multi-agent self-review pipelines with human review of design docs are becoming standard practice.

insights.claim: Practical ceiling on parallelism is about three or four concurrent agent sessions per human before context is lost, since agents finish faster than the human can track.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: The human attention bottleneck, not model speed, caps individual throughput.

insights.claim: Code review shifts toward tests and golden expectations, and stacked PRs must be reassembled and reviewed one by one by a human or they become messy; PR volume across the team rises sharply.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Review and verification capacity becomes the new constraint on AI-driven dev output.

insights.claim: Engineering leaders spend roughly 5-20% of infrastructure budgets on observability, but what they are really buying is reliability.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Observability is a proxy purchase for reliability, so it is budget that can be redirected to a better reliability product.

insights.claim: Observability cost has grown faster than output because microservices multiplied data volumes at every layer, while the marginal reliability gained per extra dollar has flattened.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Diminishing returns create a standing opening for cost-reduction and signal-extraction vendors against incumbents.

insights.claim: Greer sits in the telemetry data stream to extract signal from noise upstream, claiming plug-and-play cost reduction of about 90%, then feeds the signal into an AI layer that troubleshoots and fixes problems.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Owning the data stream is a strategic position to feed future AI ops agents.

insights.claim: Customers respond to the cost-savings pitch (saving 90% of their Datadog bill) rather than the AI reliability pitch; AI value on the ops side is harder to price than coding productivity.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Sell the concrete cost saving first and attach AI as the second layer; ops AI buyers are not yet pulling.

themes.theme: Why operations is harder than code for AI

insights.claim: Operational AI is a harder problem than code AI: production systems depend on workload, access patterns and traffic, plus hidden human knowledge and external changes, which are not in the training distribution.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Ops-focused AI startups face tougher going than code-focused ones.
insights.quote: the ones that are trying to tackle operations are having a tough go at it

insights.claim: The operational state space explodes: each added program bit doubles possible states, so reaching more states than atoms in the universe is trivial, which is why chaos engineering and product approaches to operations never worked and humans ran clusters.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Brute-force coverage of ops is infeasible; progress must come from constraining the search.
insights.quote: every time you add a bit to a program, the state space of like what it can do operationally increases by a factor of two

insights.claim: The history of systems is that smart adaptive algorithms (swap, adaptive routing, congestion control) lose to overprovisioning, implying ops may be solved by overprovisioned design rather than AI prediction.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Cheap capacity may remain the default fix, capping the market for AI ops optimization.
insights.quote: the history of systems is you don't predict stuff you overprovision because you can't

insights.claim: Models handle syntax well because they train on all code, but model quality on distributed-system trade-offs (availability, consistency, caching) is poor when behavior depends on runtime access patterns; the host called its output on a distributed Gaussian splat renderer bad.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Code generation quality does not transfer to runtime-dependent system design without grounding.

insights.claim: AI does well on query optimization when grounded in performance benchmarks and a dataset of real queries, but cannot know something like how much memory to allocate without running production experiments.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Grounding in measurable benchmarks and experiment loops is the condition for AI success in systems work.

insights.claim: Host thesis: AI takes off like wildfire in domains where the solution distribution matches the training distribution (code, images) and is far slower where the solution lives in the natural world.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Prioritize AI exposure to digital-distribution domains; physical-world domains have longer timelines and worse economics.
insights.quote: AI is going to continue to take off in a wildfire for a constrained domain

insights.claim: Self-driving is the cautionary example: after the DARPA Grand Challenge it took 20 years and $170 billion to reach worse unit economics than Uber.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Real-world AI deployment is gated by economics, not just capability.
insights.quote: it took 20 years and $170 billion of investment to get to worse unit economics than Uber

insights.claim: Most AI SRE products start from a lagging indicator (a spiked metric or alert) and backtrack to a root cause, which Jad argues is why they underperform; backtracking in complex systems is very problematic.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Competing AI SRE tools with alert-first design may have a structural accuracy limit.
insights.quote: backtracking into a root cause is actually very problematic

insights.claim: Greer instead scans petabyte-per-day logs with a separate non-LLM anomaly model, surfaces any new log pattern or change to the AI, which then reads code, checks history and tests hypotheses.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Hybrid design: deterministic or predictive models detect change, LLMs reason; LLMs are not asked to predict.
insights.quote: every time we see a new kind of pattern emerge in your logs, a new thing that we haven't seen before, we lift it up to the AI

insights.claim: Most production issues stem from some change; the heavy-tailed set of failures is large, but the set of debugging steps is manageable, so AI can emulate the human debugging workflow rather than enumerate failure states.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: AI reliability products succeed by constraining search through workflow, not by predicting rare states.

insights.claim: In Greer's early deployments, an early-warning log message that was ignored in a couple of cases later turned into production incidents, which Jad cites as validation of the detector.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Anecdotal but suggests early signal precedes incidents; sample is small.

insights.claim: The same pattern is applied to security: detect statistical perturbations such as entity cardinalities, have AI generate candidate causal chains, and verify them against the data. The host counters that adversaries intentionally seek rare states, making security harder.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Security AI faces adaptive adversaries, so ops-style results may not carry over.

insights.claim: AI cannot yet replace a human running a distributed cluster, but Jad says it is very close for query optimization and that there is enough to start the loop.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Expect query optimization to automate before full cluster operation.

themes.theme: Limits, simulation and where AI goes next

insights.claim: Jad argues code is a reduction of machine states into instructions, and he expects the ops domain to be solved by expanding complexity layer by layer, though skeptic Martin sees computational irreducibility requiring simulation or experiments.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Agents that plan their own experiments and simulations may close the gap between description and running reality.

insights.claim: Jad thinks the world may be reshaped to fit what AI can do, citing the automated data warehouse where only fully automating the whole thing worked, and expects robotics to follow the same constrain-the-environment path.
insights.speaker: Jad (CEO of Greer)
insights.so_what: Winning deployments constrain the environment so that solution set matches AI's capability.

insights.claim: Martin sees AI as a general inefficient universal function approximator whose applications will be decided by economic equilibrium, with about 30 years of value creation ahead.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: Adoption sorts by economics: where a value is monetizable AI wins first.

insights.claim: Martin believes venture is relationship, access and value-add driven, markets are efficient, and AI analysis already matches or beats the best analysts he has worked with, so AI will not replace VCs.
insights.speaker: Martin (host)
insights.so_what: AI commoditizes analysis but not access; value in VC shifts toward network and trust.
